Subject: Quick question on connectivity options for pilot

Hi Connor / Stephanie,

We're getting ready to spin up a small private deployment with Redwood for our patient-facing inference service and need a recommendation on how to connect our VPCs to Redwood's Private control plane. Our security team prioritized isolation and strict egress control, while infra wants low latency for inference (p99 < 80ms).

Can you lay out the tradeoffs between VPC peering, PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and a site-to-site VPN for our setup? We're planning a pilot in us-west-2 and want something that minimizes blast radius, supports auditability (flows + logs), and won't block a go-live in 4–6 weeks.

Attached is our rough network diagram and a filled security questionnaire (see attachments).

Thanks —
Samir

Hi Samir — thanks for the diagram and the questionnaire, both help a lot. High level here and then I'll follow up with a short decision matrix + recommended pilot.

Short answers:
- VPC peering: simplest for L3 reachability, low latency, but broad network visibility between VPCs (larger blast radius) and limited cross-account control (no private DNS by default across accounts without extra config). Good if you trust network isolation between accounts and want minimal hops.
- PrivateLink (interface VPC endpoints): smallest surface area — you expose a single endpoint from Aurora into our service plane; strong for per-service access, supports AWS security groups for fine-grained access, and reduces lateral access. Slightly more operational overhead (endpoint ENIs to manage) and can add a small latency overhead vs peering.
- Site-to-site VPN (IPsec): good as a fallback and for regulated customers who require on-prem gateways; more operational complexity (key rotation, tunnel monitoring), generally higher latency and less predictable under load. Works well as an encrypted transit with strict firewall controls.

I'll assemble a short matrix (latency, control, auditability, blast radius, ops work) and a pilot recommendation — planning to align with your compliance constraints. Is audit-level VPC flow logs + our control-plane request logs sufficient, or does Aurora need packet-level PCAP for early-stage debugging?

Connor O'Brien
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

Folks — adding a few operational and compliance points from my side:

1) Auditability: Aurora should be able to surface token-level request metadata (customer request id, model/version, route) from Redwood's console. For network-level audit, VPC flow logs combined with transit gateway flow logs (if they use a TGW) is acceptable for our SOC2 posture; packet captures are not required except for one-off debug sessions.

2) Least privilege: PrivateLink is attractive because it maps to a single service endpoint; security can lock it down with SGs and endpoint policies. If Aurora wants to maintain strict tenant isolation, PrivateLink + per-tenant endpoint policies is the pattern I recommend.

3) Latency: VPC peering will generally be the lowest-latency path for same-region VPCs, but if Aurora plans cross-account peering with a centralized shared services VPC, watch for asymmetric routing and NAT egress. PrivateLink does add a small TCP/TLS termination and ENI hop — typically 5–15ms extra depending on topology.

4) Operational: VPNs are heavier but useful as a disaster recovery fallback or for initial onboarding when customers don't want to open VPC-level peering. If we do a PrivateLink pilot, we should also test a VPN fallback in parallel to validate failover behavior.

Ben — can you sketch the minimal PrivateLink architecture + endpoint policy we'd hand to Aurora? Kimberly, please call out any SNAT/NAT considerations for egressing to Redwood's model-serving plane.

— Stephanie
Stephanie Nguyen
Head of Solutions Architecture | Redwood Inference

From: ben_carter@redwood.ai

Date: 2026-10-19T10:40:00-07:00
Subject: RE: Quick question on connectivity options for pilot

Attaching a concise design note (redwood_plink_design_notes.docx) — highlights below.

Design highlights:
- Pilot uses AWS Interface Endpoint (PrivateLink) in Aurora's VPC in us-west-2. Aurora creates an ENI-backed endpoint per-subnet (3 AZs) with endpoint policy restricting to only the inference service API.
- Security Groups: allow only the subnets/ports from Aurora's app tier. Endpoint policy blocks any other service actions.
- Egress handling: we recommend Aurora set explicit SNAT so egress to other AWS services goes through their NAT/Gateway; Redwood will respect client source IPs in the control plane logs (we include connection metadata).
- Latency expectation: +8ms median overhead observed in similar pilots (us-west-2), p99 depends on AZ placement.
- Fallback plan: configure a pair of IPsec tunnels to a small Aurora-managed VPN gateway. BGP is optional — static routes OK for pilot. Test failover with simulated endpoint interruption.

Operational checklist included in the docx: endpoint creation ARN template, SG examples, test curl commands, and monitoring hooks (CloudWatch metrics + Redwood console webhook).

Ben Carter
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
